author: Philip K. Dick
card_summary: A condensed 1978 statement in which Dick lays out the two-source cosmology of his Exegesis: a rational creator-deity and a counterfeit demiurge whose defective world traps sparks of a hidden, awakening God.
page_summary:
Written near the end of the 1970s, "Cosmogony and Cosmology" distills the sprawling metaphysics Dick had been working out privately since the 2-3-74 experiences into a compact, almost systematic essay. Dick describes reality as generated by two sources: a genuine, rational deity and a blind or deranged artificer whose creation is a flawed, deteriorating simulation. Fragments of the true God lie scattered and asleep within this counterfeit world, and history is the slow process by which those fragments recognize one another and reintegrate.

The essay reads as Dick's attempt to give his Exegesis speculations a public, argumentative shape rather than a diaristic one. He draws on Gnostic and Neoplatonic vocabulary, information theory, and his own recurring images (the black iron prison, the palm-tree garden, the hologram) to argue that the universe is a kind of encrypted message gradually decoding itself.

For readers of the Exegesis, this piece is one of the clearest map-keys to Dick's late theology, stating in a few pages what the notebooks circle for thousands. It pairs closely with the portal's Exegesis materials and with "How to Build a Universe."
